contributions.statement: Treat host ignore files (.cursorignore and similar), command allowlists and permission-required settings as convenience filters, not a security boundary: keep secrets and personal data extracts out of every directory an agent can reach, and enforce deny rules at the OS, container or credential level.
contributions.evidence: §3.2 C4: 8.4% of security posts report broken explicit constraints such as a bypassed .cursorignore, 7.1% unauthorized command execution (e.g. a git commit not on the allowlist), and 2.0% ignored permission-required settings (Claude Code auto-committing mid-session). §1 Fig. 1: the authors reproduced one report, in which Copilot read and tried to modify a restricted .env. Developer-reported and unverified, host versions and configurations not given, counts are discussion frequency rather than rates.
relative_to: 2608.23550 compile instruction-file security rules into host permission deny/ask and sandbox rules
2605.11229 a command allowlist or env filter on a CI agent does not protect secrets held by the agent process

contributions.statement: Before relying on a host's secret-file exclusion, test it with a canary: put a fake credential in a file the host is configured to exclude, run a multi-turn debugging session on code that uses it (for example a failing database connection), and fail the host setup if the agent reads or edits the file.
contributions.evidence: §1 Fig. 1: in the authors' reproduction, Copilot respected the restriction at first but read and tried to modify the .env after two consecutive debugging prompts on a database connection issue. This is a single reproduction on one host, with no version, settings or repeat count.
relative_to: 2608.23550 inventory which instruction-level rules have a matching host control
canary or honeytoken files (established security practice)

contributions.statement: Run analysis-only and codebase-question agents with write, shell and git tools removed by host or OS permissions, not with an 'analysis only, no code changes' instruction.
contributions.evidence: §3.2 C1 and C2: a developer reports the agent editing code about half the time despite 'root cause analysis only, no code changes allowed', and another reports Cursor pushing despite a 'NEVER push code to GitHub' rule. Self-reported anecdotes with no rates.
relative_to: 2608.23550 security rules written in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md are unenforced

contributions.statement: Scope agent memory, chat history and agent-written knowledge files (findings, notes) to one repository or project, and do not let a discovery agent read another project's captured notes by default.
contributions.evidence: §3.3 C10: cross-session data leakage in 4.6% of privacy posts and cross-conversation context contamination in 4.1%, including content from one project appearing in another project's FINDINGS.md. §4 S9: memory or context isolation suggested in 56 comments. Anecdotal, untested.
relative_to: context and tenant isolation, purpose limitation (ISO/IEC 29100, cited by the paper)

reason: The paper is a careful catalogue of developer-reported failure modes, but nothing in it is measured as a rate or tested as a fix. What survives is a hypothesis that host-native ignore and permission settings, not just instruction text, fail under multi-turn use, backed by one author reproduction. A canary test is the cheap way for the team to check that on each host it uses.
